questions.prompt: You are preparing the title for a law-firm style corporate health check. Return a concise title in the form: 'Corporate Health Check – [Corporation Name]'. Use the corporation’s legal name from the documents; if uncertain, use the most recent article or annual return.
Return the name of the client if it appears in the engagement or cover materials. If no separate client name is evident, repeat the corporation’s legal name. Text only.

From all documents, identify the corporation’s legal name. Prefer the name stated in the Articles of Incorporation or most recent Annual Return. If multiple versions exist, choose the most recent and briefly note any prior names in parentheses.

Identify the jurisdiction and governing statute under which the corporation is incorporated (e.g., 'Province of Nova Scotia – Companies Act' or 'Canada – Canada Business Corporations Act'). Base your answer on the Articles of Incorporation or equivalent formation document.

Generate a short phrase describing for whom this report is prepared, in the form 'Board of Directors of [Corporation Name]' or 'Shareholders of [Corporation Name]'. If the audience is unclear, use 'Management and owners of [Corporation Name]'.
Return the law firm name and practice group in the form 'McInnes Cooper – MC Corporate Health / Corporate Services Team'.
Return today’s date in long form, e.g., 'December 2, 2025', based on the system date. Text only.
If a file or matter number appears explicitly in the documents, return it as printed. Otherwise, return 'To be completed by firm' and do not fabricate a number.

In 3–5 sentences, provide an overall assessment of the corporation’s corporate health based solely on the records reviewed. Mention whether core constitutional documents are present, whether records appear generally up to date, and whether there are material gaps or risks. Use neutral, professional legal tone.

Produce 3–6 <li> items identifying the main strengths or positive aspects of the corporation’s records (e.g., 'Articles and general by-law located and internally consistent', 'Recent annual returns on file'). Each item must be one sentence, concise, and specific.
In 1–2 sentences, introduce the key deficiencies section, for example: 'Based on the documents reviewed, the following deficiencies and risk areas were identified in the corporation’s records.'

Produce 3–8 <li> items summarizing the most significant deficiencies or risks at a high level (e.g., missing annual returns, incomplete registers, unclear share issuances). Each item should be one sentence and should not rely on cross-references to numbered sections.

State the corporation’s legal name exactly as shown in the Articles of Incorporation or most recent Annual Return. If there is a discrepancy between documents, give the most recent name and note earlier names in parentheses.

State the jurisdiction and statute of incorporation (e.g., 'Nova Scotia – Companies Act (NSCA)' or 'Canada – Canada Business Corporations Act (CBCA)'). Base your answer on the formation document. If unclear, state the jurisdiction only.
Extract the incorporation or corporate access number, or similar registry number, if present. If none is found, return 'Not clearly stated in documents reviewed.'
Extract the date of incorporation or formation. Use the date format 'YYYY-MM-DD'. If several dates appear, choose the incorporation date from the Articles or certificate.
Extract the registered office address from the most recent filing or document that specifies it. Provide the address on a single line.
If a fiscal year-end is explicitly stated, return it in the form 'December 31'. If it is not stated, return 'Not specified in documents reviewed.'
Identify any historical names, trade names, or name changes referenced in the documents. If none are mentioned, return 'None noted.'

Create one <tr>...</tr> row per person who appears to be or to have been a director. For each director, populate the columns in order: (1) Name, (2) Address (city/province only, if available), (3) Position (e.g., 'Director', 'Chair of the Board'), (4) Appointment date (approximate if necessary), (5) Cessation date (if applicable; otherwise '—'), (6) Key source(s) (e.g., '2019 Annual Return'; 'Board minutes 2020-09-10'). Use concise text and do not exceed one line per cell.

In 2–4 sentences, summarize any notable observations or inconsistencies relating to directors, such as differences between Annual Returns and minutes, missing resignation dates, or apparent gaps in board composition. If everything appears consistent, say so explicitly.

Create one <tr>...</tr> row per person who appears to be or to have been an officer. For each officer, populate: (1) Name, (2) Office held (e.g., 'President', 'Secretary', 'CFO'), (3) Appointment date, (4) Cessation date (if applicable; otherwise '—'), (5) Key source(s) (e.g., 'By-Law No. 1'; 'Board minutes 2019-01-15'). Use concise text and one line per cell.

In 2–4 sentences, summarize issues relating to officer appointments and records, such as whether officer positions listed in the by-laws are actually filled, whether there are minutes documenting appointments, and any discrepancies between minutes and registers. If records seem complete and consistent, say so.

Summarize the authorized share capital as set out in the Articles or equivalent document. Describe each class (e.g., voting/non-voting, common/preferred) and any key rights or restrictions in 2–6 sentences.

Based on all documents reviewed (resolutions, registers, annual returns), summarise the issued and outstanding shares for each class, including quantities. If the information is incomplete or inferred, state the assumptions and note that the figures are based on partial records.

Provide a short narrative summary (1–2 paragraphs) of the apparent shareholder structure: identify any controlling or majority shareholders, mention whether shares appear concentrated or widely held, and note where information is inferred or incomplete.

In 3–6 sentences, identify issues or risks in the share capital and ownership records, such as absence of a formal share register, missing share certificates or resolutions, or inconsistencies between resolutions, registers, and returns. Make clear, neutral recommendations (e.g., 'A formal share register should be prepared or updated to reflect the current shareholdings.').

Produce a set of <li> items listing the main categories of documents present in the minute book, for example: 'Articles of Incorporation dated [date]', 'General By-Law No. 1', 'Board minutes 2019–2022 (selected meetings)', 'Annual Returns for 2019–2020'. Keep each item to one line.

In 2–4 sentences, describe the state of the registers and ledgers (share register, director register, officer register, securities register, etc.). Indicate which are present, which appear incomplete, and which are missing, and suggest appropriate remedial steps.

Summarise any other significant corporate records or agreements located (e.g., shareholders’ agreement, banking resolutions, option plans). Note their existence and general subject matter but do not provide detailed legal analysis.

Provide a concise prose summary (1–2 paragraphs) of the annual returns and other key corporate filings visible in the minute book, including the years for which returns are present and any notable gaps. If no returns are found, say so clearly.

In 3–5 sentences, assess the corporation’s apparent good standing based solely on the documents reviewed. Highlight any missing or late returns, any discrepancies between internal records and what would be expected by statute, and recommend confirming status directly with the corporate registry where appropriate.

Populate the deficiencies table with one <tr>...</tr> per identified deficiency. Each row must include: (1) Ref. – a short reference like 'D-1', 'D-2', etc.; (2) Area – a concise area label (e.g., 'Filings', 'Registers', 'Share Capital', 'Minutes'); (3) Deficiency / Risk – 1–3 sentences describing the issue; (4) Recommended Action – 1–2 sentences describing the specific remedial step (e.g., 'prepare and file outstanding annual returns for 2021–2023'); (5) Priority – 'High', 'Medium', or 'Low'. Focus on concrete, actionable items.

Create one <tr>...</tr> row per document reviewed. Each row should include: (1) Ref. – a short reference like 'A-1', 'A-2', etc.; (2) Document – a concise description (e.g., 'Articles of Incorporation', 'General By-Law No. 1', 'Board minutes – 2019-01-15'); (3) Date – the document date if known; otherwise 'n/a'; (4) Notes – any brief clarifying information (e.g., 'scanned copy', 'undated draft'). Keep descriptions short and professional.
